title: Prove The Mountains Move
summary: Albert Wolski speaks about EXEK’s experimental writing methods, field recordings, film scores and the making of the band’s DFA-released album Prove The Mountains Move.
transcript:
Albert Wolski of EXEK joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios to discuss Prove The Mountains Move, EXEK's album on DFA Records, ahead of its launch at the Curtin. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 12 March 2026. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Towards the end of last year you put out Live at Triple R, a special live recording made here, with a beautiful cover, Albert, of you and Joe Brnadic in an embrace. It was wonderful to see. And we should welcome you to the studio as well.

Albert: Yeah. Clara took that photo, and I was like, oh, that's got to be it. That's got to be the cover.

Lauren: It's a beautiful moment, beautifully captured by Clara. And we're embracing you metaphorically into the studio, so thank you so much for joining us.

Albert: Thanks for having us.

Simon: Of course. By way of introduction: EXEK is your project, Albert. You write and record everything in a solitary state before assembling a band to play it live, and together you've become a foundational pillar of the city's modern underground scene, with regular tours across the world, and seven albums in 10 years, so a really prolific work ethic. And as Lauren mentioned, very notably, the newest, Prove The Mountains Move, came out on DFA Records, which is such a huge deal: such an iconic modern label. It's a bit of a storied anecdote now, but could you tell anyone who hasn't heard how it all came to be?

Albert: Literally just hit him up on Instagram, sent him a message. If you ask, you might receive.

Lauren: That's the motto of the music industry, isn't it? It's very accommodating.

Albert: True. So it kind of worked out in our favour this time.

Simon: How long did you sit on that thought before you actioned it?

Albert: I gave the record to our Euro booker first, and I was like, can you do it? I don't want to do this. So he sent it out to a few labels, didn't hear anything, and I was like, okay, I might try my luck with DFA, let's go. Then I heard back from him, and they were like, shoot it through. And I was like, okay, cool. And that's what happened.

Lauren: It's a beautiful story. And it turns out they were already huge fans.

Albert: Yeah, they got the last record, and I guess they'd been kind of tracking us for a little bit. That was nice.

Simon: You've said you'd always enjoyed DFA releases, and their iconic hand-drawn lightning-bolt logo. There are some overlapping record collections too, wouldn't you say, with EXEK and DFA?

Albert: Yeah, 100%. I think we share the same kind of ancestry, whereas they might go a little bit more dancey, and we kind of go a bit more, I don't know where we go. I'm bad at that question. I'm like, oh, what do you sound like? I don't know. I don't know. Everything.

Lauren: Love that. You've said this record is experimental in its craft, but it may not necessarily sound experimental. That's an interesting distinction. What does it mean?

Albert: I guess the way that we write, people might see it as being quite backwards: we don't come up with chords and lyrics and a melody first. I always start with the drums, kind of work back from that. Start with the drums, then do the bass, then find some melodies on top of that, which might seem counterintuitive to a lot of songwriting, but it seems to work for us, and we really value the drum sound a lot. I spend a lot of time affecting the drums and making them sound maybe a little more unique than other records you hear these days.

Simon: So it's always music first for you, and then the lyrics. You said a while ago that lyrics are just sounds, which I find so interesting, because EXEK lyrics are so evocative and poetic. Is that something you still feel?

Albert: Oh, 100%. I kind of just phonetically sound out where and what it should sound like, and then I find the words I can fit in there, and then I've pieced together some kind of a narrative, or some kind of cohesion, between all these vowel sounds and consonants and alliteration and rhyme and stuff like that. So I kind of just go off that.

Lauren: Lyrics and vocal delivery do seem quite important to unlocking the sound of this particular record. We read some interviews where you talked about hearing Pearl Jam and Sheryl Crow and the Go-Go's at 2am house parties and clubs, and being really struck by the pull of a simple vocal melody. What did those experiences unlock for you on this record?

Albert: It made me want to sing a bit more. EXEK kind of started off as almost an instrumental band where, like I said, we value drums and rhythm a lot more than song structure. So now I'm pushing myself into, all right, let's get some hooks in here. Let's get some ABBA going in here. Let's see what happens.

Lauren: Is that the motto in the studio?

Albert: Yeah, big time.

Lauren: And how's that feeling for you?

Albert: It's great. It's like unlocking some doors and opening some windows. See where it goes.

Lauren: Let the wind in. We heard you were comparing your mixes against the Beatles' Abbey Road. Is that right?

Albert: Yeah. I've got all the tracks lined up in a session, and then I just have some Abbey Road sitting underneath it, muted. And I'm like, all right, cool, let's A/B that against Abbey Road. See how that sits. I wish I was doing that like 10 years ago.

Simon: All good things come after time, I suppose. And you've worked out a nice system for yourself.

Albert: Yeah. I'm still working it out.

Lauren: You've also mentioned Barbra Streisand, Mariah Carey, Celine Dion and Coldplay as influences.

Albert: Somewhat, yeah. Somewhat.

Simon: Is there a particular story behind 'Arrivederci Back Pain'?

Albert: No, I don't think there is. Oh, actually, the drums are from Pulp's 'This Is Hardcore'.

Simon: Did you catch Pulp when they were here recently?

Albert: No, I didn't see that. I've seen them before. I saw them at Primavera, about 15 years ago, and that was great. I didn't really like the last record that much; it didn't really grab me. But I liked the one before that, the one they did with Scott Walker, a lot.

Simon: So there's a bit of Pulp in this one?

Albert: Yeah, the drums, that's 'This Is Hardcore'. And then with the guitar riff I just kind of wanted to make something that was not 'This Is Hardcore'. And then it just evolved organically, with a middle eight that turned into almost a whole other song, in terms of going somewhere else.

Lauren: We understand you're a big cinephile as well: your honours thesis was on the scores for films like Under the Skin and Videodrome. In those films it's hard to tell where the score ends and the sound design begins, which feels connected to how EXEK recordings work, with household items and field recordings sitting alongside synths and guitars. How does that film-scoring thinking shape what you do?

Albert: You guys really did your research. I just find it interesting when the score is between diegetic and non-diegetic. You can't really trust it. I like it when you just kind of trust your environment. It really opens a few doors, and I try to do that a little bit with EXEK.

I haven't been doing it that much lately, but I might go back to it. There's a little bit of that on the latest record: on the last song there are some tram noises and some rain, to make it seem a bit more ambient. I think that's just a bit of fun to have, to make your studio the world. I also record a lot at home sometimes, with the windows open and stuff.

'Cause I don't really think that you need to record everything in absolute silence. 'Cause no one's going to listen to it in absolute silence. It doesn't really matter. So to have some birds deep in the background is totally fine, or some tram noises, or some chitter-chatter from the neighbours. I enjoy that. It kind of builds a narrative.

Simon: It gives us a space to inhabit. A bit of an incidental question, but you did mention rain sounds, and in previous interviews we've heard you talk about the prominence of water, as both a sound and a concept, in your records. Is that something that you —

Albert: I think that's 'cause I'm a Cancerian. I don't know. It's all in there. Tsunami dreams: I've got tidal waves and big, big waves happening. And tsunamis and stuff. So I just kind of tackle that.

Lauren: Huge elemental forces at play.

Albert: Elemental forces. And I'm just trying to be my own psychologist and psychiatrist.

Lauren: Have you looked up what tsunami dreams mean?

Albert: Yeah. I think it's time-related, and feeling a little bit out of control, which in this day and age can be applied to everyone.

Simon: Truly. Well, you're harnessing these forces for extraordinary art and music, for good, not evil. The press release for the new record talks about an experimental chiropractor at Changi Airport, dust bunnies at a food court, spray bottles and glass-bottom boats. How do you think about the themes and stories on this album?

Albert: It just comes back to how I write at first, phonetically sounding out stuff, then going back and trying to get some kind of a narrative going. And then if I can piece it all together, have a bit of a story from start to end, or just a bit of a glimpse or a vignette into my cuckoo head, then yeah, that's it.

Simon: Speaking of inspiration, we also read that you follow science journals like New Scientist. Do many lyrics emerge from that space?

Albert: They used to. Not so much anymore. Every now and again I'm in a supermarket, and I'm like, oh, New Scientist. I haven't fucking picked that up in a while.

Lauren: Dive in.

Albert: Yeah. I've got to dive in and use that for influence. But I think I've just been going inside my own head a bit more than the world at large.

Lauren: Excavating. We wanted to quickly mention the artwork too, which is really gorgeous. Is there any significance to the goat and the sports car on the cover?

Albert: That was just something that my wife snapped in Crete. There's this beach with these goats that just hang out in the car park, but also right on the beach. I think it's called something like Seitan Beach or something, in Crete. Very picturesque, and on top of it, it looks like a bit of a moonscape. There are just these goats that will spoil everyone's picnic and get your chips out of your mouth.

Lauren: That's amazing. It's up there with the cover of yourself and Joe in the embrace, with the photo taken by Clara, of course, from Velvet Haze. EXEK are launching Prove The Mountains Move this Saturday at the Curtin, which I think you called your spiritual home. What does that venue mean to the band?

Albert: I feel like every time we need to put out a record, we've got to play there. Why not?

Simon: Incredible venue, beautiful room, great people who work there. And you're supporting LCD Soundsystem in Boston. That's coming up for you too.

Albert: Yeah. It was supposed to be Philly as well, but that got cancelled, unfortunately. So I just get to do four in Boston with them, and then a few of our own shows. I was looking forward to it just being this easy tour, with four shows in Boston and then four in Philly. And I was like, cool, that's it, that's a wrap. I'm just going to park myself in the city for four days. Not have to soundcheck. I don't know, I'm kind of making this up. If I've soundchecked the first night, why would I need to soundcheck the second and third and fourth if nothing's changed? So I was looking forward to that, and I still am. Obviously Boston's happening; Philly isn't.

Lauren: Is there a New York show as well?

Albert: I think we might be doing two New York shows. We've got one that we've announced, and we're going to do one in Philly as well, just ourselves.

Simon: We hope it's smooth sailing. Thanks so much, Albert, for joining us on Breaking and Entering.
